**Dev learning:** In Apple's vocabulary CANCELLATION means **auto-renew was switched off**. Access continues to `expires_date`; EXPIRATION is what ends it. We mapped it to a status our tier resolver rejects. And because I'd recommended creating the charity offer with auto-renew off — for good reasons, so nobody gets charged £59.99 mid-marathon-taper — RevenueCat emits CANCELLATION about two minutes after **every single redemption**. In the measured case both events landed in the same second, and the ordering guard faithfully applied the newer one. All 500 runners would have dropped to free tier minutes after redeeming.
**Product/creator learning:** The config decision and its downstream consequence lived in two different systems and I only reasoned about one. I argued auto-renew off convincingly on reputational grounds and never asked what event that causes. **A configuration choice is a code path.**
**AI-building learning:** Both unit tests were green and both were right. One asserted `CANCELLATION -> 'cancelled'`. The other asserted the tier resolver grants paid on `['trialing','active']`. Nothing anywhere ran the output of the first into the second, so nobody ever asked the only question that matters: *after this event, does the runner still have access?* This repo's own ship checklist has that rule — test the composed path — with no mechanical enforcement for this pair. Writing the composition test took ten minutes and it went red immediately.
**The honest bit:** The sweep for the same shape found Stripe doing it too: `past_due` mapped to `expired`, which revokes a customer **while Stripe is still retrying their card**. The reasoning against exactly that was already written down in the RevenueCat file, two lines above the bug. Nobody had carried it across. It was also impossible to test where it lived — a private function in an `app/` route, and vitest only collects `lib/`. Untestable code is where the untested bugs are, which is not a coincidence.
**Hook material:** "Cancelled" doesn't mean cancelled. Apple sends CANCELLATION when someone turns off auto-renew — and if you create a free offer code with auto-renew off, it fires on every redemption, two minutes after the purchase.
**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-28 — CHARITY-OFFER-CODE-01 · paid at Apple, free in our app
**Shipped:** An Apple offer code redeemed before the runner has an account now actually reaches their account.
**Dev learning:** The failure was four steps long and every one of them looked fine on its own. App boots signed out, so RevenueCat gets an anonymous id. The SDK syncs the Apple receipt and fires `INITIAL_PURCHASE` — an event we handle correctly. The handler passes the id to Postgres, which answers `invalid input syntax for type uuid`. The route returns 500, RevenueCat retries, and **every retry fails identically because the id never becomes valid on its own.** I only found it by running the RPC against production with an anonymous id to see what it actually said. **Reading the code would not have told me; the database did.**
**Product/creator learning:** I gave the founder two contradictory answers before this — first "you need a new build and App Review", then "actually web redemption works today". Both were half right and the second was only reachable because I checked what Capacitor actually does: the app loads from `server.url`, so **JS and server changes ship on push**, and the RevenueCat plugin already has the redemption sheet compiled in. The schedule risk I'd put in front of him didn't exist. **When the answer changes, say which part was wrong and why, not just the new answer.**
**AI-building learning:** The tempting version of the fix is to let the app read `customerInfo` and tell the server "I'm entitled". That is a free subscription for anyone who can call an endpoint. The app says *re-check me*; the server asks RevenueCat with a secret the client never holds. The other discipline that mattered: the route **refuses rather than grants** when it cannot verify — and records that it refused, so a missing API key is distinguishable from "nobody redeemed a code". Silence would have looked identical to success right up until 500 people complained.
**The honest bit:** An existing test explicitly listed `TRANSFER` and `PRODUCT_CHANGE` as events we deliberately don't understand. I reversed that. It was a recorded decision and reversing it silently would have been the worst version of this change, so the reason now sits in the test next to the assertion. And the thing I keep having to say: **this is fixed in code and unproven in reality.** It needs a sandbox offer code on a real device, and nothing here substitutes for that.
**Hook material:** "A charity runner redeems a free year. Apple says yes. Our database says `invalid input syntax for type uuid`. Our server says 500. RevenueCat retries forever. The runner sees a paywall."
**Postable?:** yes — the four-step silent failure is vivid, and "the client never asserts entitlement" is a security point worth making.

## 2026-09-28 — NAV-FADE-CONTRAST-01 · the check I said hadn't run, run
**Shipped:** The receded nav's labels darken so they stay readable over whatever scrolls under them.
**Dev learning:** I closed the previous ruling with "the lozenge has not been measured against the receded, blurred bar — a re-measure, not a re-ruling." The founder asked for that measure and it failed. A translucent bar's labels do not sit on the bar; they sit on **whatever is behind it**. Over our own grounds it passed (4.69–4.86). Over a moss CTA it was **3.58:1**, and the AA boundary turned out to be a backdrop of grey **220** — a light grey, not some extreme. Reachable that same day, because `TODAY-CTA-CLEARANCE-01` was reverted and the moss "Log this session" button scrolls straight under the bar.
**Product/creator learning:** The fix was free, and only because of the change I shipped four hours earlier. Making the selected state depend on a lozenge and a weight instead of colour meant the receded state was suddenly **free to repaint both labels**. Neither sitting predicted that the two would need each other. The alternative — raising the bar's opacity — measured at **alpha 0.93**, which is an opaque bar: it would have answered "a bit opaque" by deleting the thing he asked for.
**AI-building learning:** The original amendment's "blur holds ≥5.23:1 worst case" was not wrong so much as **under-scoped** — measured against our palette rather than against content, and I built on it without re-deriving it. The durable output is not the token, it's the gate's **scope**: the check now measures the worst possible backdrop rather than the surfaces we happen to ship. That is the same population-failure class as the untracked file this morning and the clock-dependent fixtures, in a third place.
**The honest bit:** I introduced the defect and shipped it live for a few hours. Then, fixing it, I wrote the registry row and the state blocks and **forgot the build-log entry entirely** — pushed, and `audit-docs.sh` caught it as "registry=1 buildlog=0, a ship lost its records". Second time today a hook caught my record-keeping rather than my code. This entry exists because the check does.
**Hook material:** "The accessibility claim said 5.23:1 worst case. It had been measured against our own colours, not against the content that scrolls underneath. The real worst case was 2.67."
**Postable?:** yes — "your contrast check is only as good as the backgrounds you tested it against" is concrete and widely applicable.

## 2026-09-28 — NAV-ACTIVE-LOZENGE-01 + NAV-FADE-01 · the nav did not say where you were
**Shipped:** The selected tab now has a lozenge and a heavier label, and the bar recedes while you scroll.
**Dev learning:** He sent two screenshots and said he liked how you can tell which page is selected. I nearly treated that as a styling brief. The measurement made it something else entirely: our active label and our inactive label have **identical relative luminance** — 1.00:1, zero greyscale separation. The only thing distinguishing "you are here" from "you are not" was hue. We had `aria-current="page"`, so a screen reader was fine, and a sighted colour-blind runner had nothing at all. **Aria does not discharge 1.4.1** — that rule is about visual presentation, and `ui-patterns.md` already held us to *"state must live in the label, never colour alone"*.
**Product/creator learning:** Two thirds of what he was admiring was already shipped or already ruled. The floating pill went live three days ago; the recede he asked for on the 25th was ruled and then sat unbuilt. **The settled-ground scan turned a four-item wishlist into one new question and one overdue build** — and that is the second time today reading the register changed the answer rather than confirming it.
**AI-building learning:** The register said a fill cannot work on this palette, measured, four rounds spent, founder shown an A/B and seeing nothing. It would have been very easy — and wrong — to quote that and decline. The finding was about a fill fighting **two** grounds; a lozenge inside the bar has **one**. Recomputing took a minute and produced a usable window with a hard ceiling at 0.08. **A measured impossibility is scoped to what was measured**, and the discipline is to check whether your case is the same case.
**The honest bit:** The pre-commit hook blocked my first commit for hex literals in the test file — including one inside an explanatory comment. It was right twice: the fix was not to de-hex the comment but to read the colour **whole from the token**, so the gate cannot drift if the value is retuned. That is the third time today a guard caught something I had written while writing a guard.
**Hook material:** "Our app told you which page you were on using a colour that is exactly as bright as the one it was contrasted against. 1.00:1. The accessibility attribute was perfect and the pixels said nothing."
**Postable?:** yes — the identical-luminance measurement is vivid, checkable, and the kind of thing most teams have somewhere.

## 2026-09-28 — OPS-ATTRIB-01 + OPS-FUNNEL-02 + W-TRUST-01 · I broke nine things with one regex
**Shipped:** A one-tap attribution row, four events on the two shipped restraint artifacts, a named source on every paywall door, and one true sentence on the homepage.
**Dev learning:** I substituted `setScreen('upgrade')` across a 7,800-line file by regex — and the explanatory comment I had inserted three lines earlier **quoted that same string in backticks**. So the comment consumed the first label, the new helper consumed the second, all nine paywall doors were attributed to the wrong screen, two got no label at all, and the helper ended up calling itself. **`tsc` passed the whole time.** The repo has this exact rule written down three times — *"bound the region, never grep the file"* — and I hit it a fourth way nobody had: not a substring collision in the code, but in my own documentation of the code. The only reason I caught it is that I printed a straggler count and it said 2 instead of 0.
**Product/creator learning:** Asked whether we were making the most of two shipped features, the measurement killed the obvious answer. "It's stuck behind a paywall" is false — 13 of 27 accounts can already reach paid surfaces, and only 2 have a scored weekly report. The constraint was never the tier; it was report generation and HR availability. **Two hours of UX opinions would have optimised the wrong step.**
**AI-building learning:** The Design Board is worth more than I expected when it constrains rather than approves. Every line of the attribution row is a ruling: no Moss, no icon, no typing, renders last, says who benefits. I would have written a friendlier, more colourful, more "helpful" row and it would have been worse. And the board's **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** on the reshape hero saved me building a section the register had already declined five days earlier in favour of `SameWeekTwice` — I'd called it "the best idea in the paper" before reading the component's header.
**The honest bit:** Three self-inflicted things in one sitting. The regex above. Then `[...matchAll()]`, which CLAUDE.md warns about by name in its TypeScript section. Then I nearly cited `weekly_reports.opened_at` as "0 reports opened" to a board — a column that nothing in the codebase writes. That last one is the same mistake I made this morning with the webhook ops events, twice in one day, and both times what saved me was checking whether the thing that would have written the value exists.
**Hook material:** "One regex broke nine paywall doors, made a function call itself, and the type checker was perfectly happy." Also: only 2 of 27 users could see the feature we were about to write marketing copy for.
**Postable?:** yes — the regex-matched-my-own-comment story is specific, embarrassing and genuinely useful, and it has a clean moral.

## 2026-09-28 — OPS-SUBS-ALERT-01 · I filed the bug wrong and the real one was worse
**Shipped:** A runner who pays and doesn't get access now has a named, severity-ordered, tested place in the daily digest — and the repo fails the build if a new payment provider's failure kinds go unclassified.
**Dev learning:** I filed this as "nothing alerts on these rows". Then I read the digest routine and Q4 turned out to be a **generic 24-hour feed over ops_events with no kind filter** — the rows were already arriving. The actual defect was three narrower things, and each is worse than the headline I'd written: they landed under "engine health: constitutional findings", which is the wrong heading for money; Q4's columns are engine-shaped so every field my trace records rendered as `-` (the kind appeared, the diagnosis didn't); and the window was 24 hours, so a Saturday failure was gone by Monday. **"Nothing looks" and "something looks in the wrong place with the wrong columns" need different fixes** — the second doesn't want a probe, it wants a query.
**Product/creator learning:** The best line in the whole change is a rule I switched OFF. The digest has a hard-won discipline of ageing findings against the running deployment so it never reports a fixed bug in the present tense. For this one section that rule is wrong: **a lost sale is still lost after the code is fixed.** The row is still missing and the runner is still locked out. Encoding the exception, with the reason, was more valuable than the query.
**AI-building learning:** Two near-misses, both caught by reading rather than testing. First: I nearly shipped without touching STEP 4, which builds the HTML dashboard he actually opens — the query would have run and the dashboard would still have shown nothing. Second, the good one: my completeness test originally asserted the kind list's contents, which is a tautology. Rewriting it to **derive** what the list must contain by asking `webhookTrace` what each provider can emit meant exporting the provider array, because **a TypeScript union cannot be iterated** — a test written against the type would have passed forever while a third provider went unclassified. The test now fails the build on provider drift, which is the only version of it worth having.
**The honest bit:** I rewrote an 18KB prompt in a live unattended automation by retyping it, which is exactly the kind of thing that corrupts silently. I only got away with it because I saved the original, diffed my intended version first, then read the live prompt back and compared byte-for-byte (21,430 = 21,430, all three internal copies in sync). If I hadn't verified, a dropped query in someone's daily ops tooling would have been invisible for weeks. And the thing I shipped still isn't gated: the surfacing lives in a cloud prompt, so if anyone edits the routine and drops Q9, nothing in the repo fails.
**Hook material:** "I filed the bug, then read the code and found my own bug report was wrong — and the real defect was worse: the alert was firing into a section titled 'engine health' with every useful column blank." Also: a rule I deliberately switched off — a lost sale is still lost after the code is fixed.
**Postable?:** yes — the "my own bug report was wrong" angle is honest and specific, and the age-against-the-build exception is a genuinely interesting ops idea.

## 2026-09-28 — TEST-CLOCK-PINSWEEP-01 · nineteen files, four dates, and the shortcut I didn't take
**Shipped:** The remaining 19 clock-dependent engine tests now generate against a pinned plan start, 68 call sites, and the debt register is empty.
**Dev learning:** The tempting version of this is one constant and a single sed. I'd already proved that wrong earlier the same day — pinning the first four to `COHORT_PLAN_START` instead of their own authoring Monday left two tests failing, because plan length is derived from weeks available and the races moved from 12 weeks out to 33. So **one week of runway can change the plan**, which means nineteen files needed their own dates, not a convenient shared one. `git log --diff-filter=A` gave each file's first commit; that clustered into four Mondays (0907, 0914, 0921, 0928). Scripted the 68 rewrites with a regex that only matches a call whose tier argument immediately closes the parens, so an already-pinned call can't be double-edited.
**Product/creator learning:** None of these 19 were failing. They were queued — 10 of them inside eight weeks of their own cliff. The interesting bit is that the failure mode isn't "test goes red", it's "assertion quietly stops being checked", and there is no symptom until a date passes. A suite with an expiry date looks exactly like a healthy one.
**AI-building learning:** I made the debt register empty and then **asserted that it's empty**. My first instinct was to leave the baseline mechanism as a place to park future offenders, which is how a register becomes a suppression list — the repo already has a note that a declared reason is not a fixed problem. Turning it from "track debt" into "forbid debt, and make adding a row a deliberate act with a written reason" cost two lines and is the difference between a gate and a ledger. Also added a floor on the discovered corpus size so the positive arm can't pass vacuously on an empty scan, which is the failure shape that caused the original incident.
**The honest bit:** I reported "19 files" all day and the real number in the class was 23 — I'd fixed 4 and counted the rest separately, which is fine, but the headline I kept using undercounted the class. And the margins I published (weeks-until-block) are a deliberately pessimistic pairing that produced two negative numbers for files that were passing perfectly well; I labelled it an upper bound rather than re-measuring properly, because the gate makes the exact number irrelevant.
**Hook material:** 68 call sites, 19 files, four different pinned dates — and the reason it couldn't be one date is that a single week of runway changes the plan. Register went 19 → 0 in one commit.
**Postable?:** maybe — it's a good companion to the previous entry rather than a post of its own; the "debt register that lived for one commit" idea is the reusable bit.

## 2026-09-28 — TEST-CLOCK-PREPTIME-01 · the tests did not break, the calendar moved
**Shipped:** Four engine test files now generate against a pinned plan start instead of `nextMonday()`, and a new gate stops a fifth appearing.
**Dev learning:** Nine tests went red on a commit that touched none of them. The fixtures hardcoded a `race_date` and passed no `planStart`, so the engine used the wall clock and the gap closed a week at a time until §44 refused to generate. **The seam was already there** — `generateRulePlan(input, tier, planStart?, catalogue?, todayOverride?)`, with both parameters documented "never passed by production callers" — and four files just never used it. The thing I'll remember: **five of the nine were not failing, they were absent.** One file reported "0 test" because it couldn't be collected, and it was the guard over an 837-session zone defect. A file that has silently stopped running looks identical to a file with nothing to say, and the test count is the only place it shows.
**Product/creator learning:** The cost of a clock-dependent test isn't the red, it's the interval where the assertion has quietly become unproven. Four real claims — is the long-run colour reachable, does the zone sheet teach the zone the header showed — were unguarded and the suite looked like it was still checking them.
**AI-building learning:** I reached for the convenient constant. `COHORT_PLAN_START` was right there, exported, already documented for exactly this class of bug — and using it puts the races 33 weeks out instead of 12, past §44's warn bound and into the foundation path. **I tried it: two tests still failed.** Had the fixtures been slightly less sensitive it would have gone green on a different plan and I'd have called it fixed. The lesson isn't "read the comment", it's that **a green suite after a fixture change proves nothing unless you know the fixture still produces the same thing.** Also: my own backlog filing said "marathon, blocks" — three of the four are 10K time-targets failing through a different throw, and a fix aimed at the block alone would have left three red. I wrote that filing four hours earlier from the stack trace of one file.
**The honest bit:** The gate I wrote to catch clock bias was immediately failed by the repo's lint against substring bias — `toContain('PINNED_PLAN_START')` also matches `PINNED_PLAN_STARTX`. Took the suggested `toMatch(/\b…\b/)` rather than the `hollow-ok` escape hatch. Separately, my background watcher for the earlier deploy reported a timeout while the deploy had been Ready for ten minutes: I'd sent stderr to `/dev/null` and the Vercel CLI prints the status table to stderr, so my predicate only ever saw a bare URL and could never match "Ready". Second check of the day that couldn't distinguish its two states. And I fixed 4 of 23 files — the other 19 are gated and baselined, not fixed, with 10 inside eight weeks of their own cliff on the pessimistic read.
**Hook material:** "Nine tests failed and the diff was empty. The calendar was the only thing that changed." Also: 3,719 → 3,728 tests, and five of the nine new ones were tests that had been silently not running.
**Postable?:** yes — "your test suite has an expiry date" is a strong, concrete angle, and the 0-test-collection detail is the part people won't have thought about.

## 2026-09-28 — OPS-SUBS-TRACE-01 + OPS-FUNNEL-01 · the pipe was fine, the middle was dark
**Shipped:** Both subscription webhooks now leave a durable row on success and on a failed write, and the upgrade screen records view → attempt → result.
**Dev learning:** The ops report said "1 active (paying), 0 trialing — trials aren't reaching the subscriptions table". Both halves of the alarm were wrong and one migration comment said so in plain English: *"our 14-day reverse trial has NO subscription row — it is driven purely by user_settings.trial_started_at."* A reverse trial creates no Apple transaction, so `trialing = 0` is correct forever, and the one "paying" row is the founder's own hand-seeded stripe row with `is_admin = true`. **Real revenue is 0 and the trial side is healthy: 27/27 rows carry `trial_started_at`, 12 inside the window.** The actual hole was between them — `analytics_events` contained exactly one event type. The other thing I nearly got wrong: I reasoned "no revenuecat ops events, therefore the webhook never fired", then read the route and found it records **nothing on success**, so absence proved nothing. The defensible claim was narrower — no `provider='revenuecat'` row has ever existed.
**Product/creator learning:** An alarm can be entirely false and still point at something real. The founder's instinct that the conversion pipe was unmeasurable was right; his stated reason for it was not. Worth separating those before building. Also: `design-rulings.md` had already killed a merchandising screen partly because *"we would be designing a funnel nobody has observed"* — the board had named this exact gap from the other side and nobody connected it to an instrumentation task.
**AI-building learning:** The reuse step earned its keep twice in ten minutes. `upgradeFraming()` already returned the exact three-state reason the funnel needed, so the event carries the same variant the screen renders instead of a second derivation — and while reading for that I found the cancel rule written twice in one file with two different predicates (`=== true` vs truthy). I would have written a third copy if I had gone straight to typing. **The consumer check also stopped me creating a defect:** new event types in `analytics_events` would have silently inflated the CO-ONE engagement gate if `v_coach_engagement` counted rows without filtering. It filters. I only know that because I opened the migration instead of assuming.
**The honest bit:** I piped `git commit` through `tail -30` on the first commit and threw away the post-commit hook output — the exact mistake this repo has a memory note about, titled "DO NOT PIPE AWAY YOUR INSTRUMENTATION". Second commit ran clean. And I shipped a named gap rather than a closed one: the trace rows land and are queryable, but **nothing alerts on them**, which N-015 says is not observability. Filed rather than pretended. Separately, the full suite is **red on a clean tree** — 9 tests across 4 files — because fixtures hardcode `race_date: '2026-12-12'` for a marathon and `enforcePrepTime` now blocks at ~75 days out. Not mine (verified by stashing), but it means four real assertions are now *unproven* rather than failing, and it gets worse every day.
**Hook material:** "435 ops rows across 13 kinds, and not one came from the code that takes the money." Also: the deletion I ran that morning moved the conversion gate's denominator from 28 to 24 — reconciled exactly as 28 − 7 purged + 3 new — so any future rate is inflated ~29% against the baseline verified three days earlier.
**Postable?:** yes — the false-alarm-pointing-at-a-real-hole angle is the strongest one, and the denominator arithmetic is a concrete self-inflicted measurement lesson.

## 2026-09-27 — SESSION-DIST-UNITS-01 · the wrong number next to the right one
**Shipped:** Distances on six surfaces now convert to the reader's units, and a long run is finally called a long run.
**Dev learning:** `SESSION_LABELS['easy']` was the only answer `getSessionLabel` could ever give, because the engine models a long run as `type: 'easy'` so the intensity ratios treat it as aerobic volume. The colour function twenty lines above it had been fixed for exactly this fifteen days earlier, with a comment saying the long-run colour had been "declared, ratified, consumed by nothing". **The remedy was applied to one twin and the other sat right underneath it.** Tenth time this repo has recorded that shape. The grep that finds it is one line and I only ran it because the exit criteria made me.
**Product/creator learning:** A user wrote in to say the AI read of his run was wrong. It wasn't — it was exactly right, and I verified it against his data. What was wrong was the distance printed directly above it, and that was enough to make him distrust the correct sentence. **A wrong number beside a right one discredits the right one.** The cost of a display bug is not the display.
**AI-building learning:** My own fix was wrong on the second pass. I routed everything through the shared formatter and the default rounds, so 7.11 miles would have rendered as "7mi" — a smaller version of the complaint I was fixing. The line I deleted used `.toFixed(1)` and that was information: measured values and prescribed values round differently, and the prompt layer already encodes that distinction in two separate functions. **The code you are replacing is evidence. Read why it did what it did before you delete it.**
**The honest bit:** Six sites, and only two of nineteen users are on miles. This has been broken for every one of them on every one of those screens, and nobody found it until a user did. We have no test for "render this as a miles user would see it", which is why the gate I added sweeps for the shape rather than checking an output.
**Hook material:** "A user told us our AI got his run wrong. It hadn't — it was right to within a tenth of a mile. The number printed above it said 11.4mi when he'd run 7.1, and that was enough." Also: 11.44 km printed as "11.4mi" for fifteen days, on six screens, for every miles user.
**Postable?:** yes — "the wrong number next to the right one" is the cleanest lesson I have had all week.

## 2026-09-27 — LOAD-DEDUPE-MANUAL-01 · both bugs I filed were wrong, and the real one was mine
**Shipped:** Manual runs now record when the run happened rather than when it was typed, and the load model stopped collapsing two real runs into one.
**Dev learning:** I added a dedup step to the load model in the morning because production had duplicate activity rows. By evening it was deleting real volume. A manual log stamped `new Date()` — the moment of typing — so two different sessions logged in one sitting had identical timestamps and identical distances, and my time-and-distance heuristic ate one. The fix is to stop guessing where an exact answer exists: the manual uuid is `manual-w{n}-{day}`, deterministic per session, so two different uuids are two different runs by construction. **Where a heuristic and an identifier disagree, the identifier wins.**
**Product/creator learning:** Both defects I filed earlier in the day were wrong, and in the same way. "88 analysis rows point at missing activities" was the demo account's seed script writing synthetic ids, plus manual rows that carry no id by design. "The same run ingested twice" was four rows from April. I filed both from a join I had not validated, while measuring something else, and in both cases the disconfirming evidence was already printed in my own probe output — every single orphan had `source: 'manual'` and I read straight past it.
**AI-building learning:** Twice today I have generated a dramatic number and not interrogated it before handing it on — 65% of runs off-plan (really 27%), and 88 orphaned analysis rows (really zero). Both times the correction was one column in output I had already produced. **The failure is not the query, it is stopping at the first number that supports the story I am telling.**
**The honest bit:** The dedup that broke this was mine, shipped hours earlier, with tests and a falsification pass. It was correct for the case I built it for — cross-source duplicates — and wrong for a case I had seen in the same probe output and not thought about. Passing tests told me nothing, because I wrote the tests from the same incomplete picture.
**Hook material:** "I shipped a fix in the morning that was deleting user data by the evening. Both bugs I filed that day turned out not to exist. The evidence that would have told me was in output I had already read." Also: real Strava ids are 11 digits; the ones I'd flagged as orphans were 9000000023, 9000000024, 9000000025 — a seed script counting upward.
**Postable?:** yes — the honest version of "I found three bugs" is "two weren't real and the third was mine", and that is a better post.

## 2026-09-27 — METRIC-TILE-01 · the card that was never there
**Shipped:** The session card's distance tile got the surface it was always meant to have, and the pace value stopped wrapping.
**Dev learning:** `SESSION_COLORS` holds CSS variables, not hex. So `` `${config.color}10` `` built the string `"var(--session-long)10"`, which no browser can parse, so the fill and border were silently dropped. **The tile has rendered bare on every session since the code was written.** Nothing errors — the element appears, just without its surface — so it is invisible to every check we have and to anyone reading the code, because the line *looks* like the alpha-hex trick that works on a literal. The correct idiom, `color-mix(in srgb, X N%, transparent)`, was already in the same file ten times, four lines above one of the broken sites.
**Product/creator learning:** The founder reported "one side is bigger than the other". That was true and it had two causes: a value wrapping to two lines, and a card that had never existed. **He could only see the symptom of the second one.** Worth remembering when a report sounds like a spacing nit — the thing being described and the thing that is wrong are not always the same object.
**AI-building learning:** My first version of the gate reported the fix's own explanatory comment as a live offender, because I did not strip comments. That is the third time this week a check has fired on prose describing the bug it guards. Then the pre-commit hook blocked the test's own negative case — a hardcoded hex inside an assertion that hex is *ignored*. Both are the same shape: **a check cannot tell the difference between the thing and a description of the thing, unless you make it.**
**The honest bit:** I have now shipped a visual change the founder has never seen — the distance tile will appear tinted with a coloured border for the first time. That might be worse than the bare version. I flagged it as an open clause rather than pretending the fix is obviously right, but I did ship it before he looked.
**Hook material:** "A card in our app was designed, reviewed, and shipped with a background and a border. It has never once rendered either. The string `var(--session-long)10` is not a colour, and no browser will tell you."

## 2026-09-27 — LOG-ONE-INTENTION-01 · the app was asking a question it could answer
**Shipped:** One button to log a run, a rest day that can log one at all, and the seven strings for "I ran" collapsed to one verb.
**Dev learning:** `handleMarkComplete()` already branched — auto-match logs against it, no match opens the picker. **The decision logic was built, correct, and ignored by the UI, which put the same choice in front of the runner anyway.** I had scoped this as "redesign the logging flow" and it was mostly deletion. The general version: before you build a decision, check whether the code already makes it and the interface is just not trusting it.

That is the same failure `brand.md` bans "Based on your data…" for. The founder's complaint was "it doesn't make that clear", and what was unclear was that we were describing our own internals on a button.
**AI-building learning:** Four separate guards in this one area anchor on something the next defect did not have — `<IconButton` tags, `onClick={onBack}`, `minWidth: '100px'`. The fourth one, `linkHierarchy.test.ts`, **failed loudly saying "anchor not found — re-anchor this test"** when I deleted the button it pointed at. That is the difference between a check that degrades safely and three that quietly matched nothing. If a check depends on an anchor, assert the anchor exists.
**The honest bit:** I built this without the mock-up the Design Board ruled for. The founder said "do all phases now" and I did, but Collins' `mock-up before code` was a real ruling on the most-used flow in the app, and nothing here has run on a device. If this feels wrong in the hand, that is why, and it is one revert away.
**Hook material:** "Seven different buttons in our app meant 'I ran'. The code already knew which one to use. The interface asked the user anyway." Also: a rest day had no way to log a run at all, on 4 of 7 days.
**Postable?:** yes — "the app was asking a question it could already answer" is the cleanest thing I have written down this week.



## 2026-09-27 — MODIFY-CONFIRM-01 · the missing back button was the symptom

"Bound the region, never grep the file" is a rule I have written into three separate files in this repo and I still did it. The test failing was the only reason I noticed — if the window had been 120 characters it would have passed and meant nothing.

## 2026-09-27 — BACKARROW-WIZARD-01 · the guard that could not see its own twin
**Shipped:** The wizard's hand-rolled back button deleted in favour of the shared one, ten `ghost` full-width CTAs given a surface, and three gates so none of it comes back.

Nobody was careless. The check was looking at a shape the defect didn't have. When you write a conformance gate, the question is not "does this catch the violations I know about" but "what shape of violation can this never express".

A ruling without a check is a suggestion with good manners.

Both mutations had silently failed to land — one targeted a Button that already carried an override so the count didn't move, the other used a regex that couldn't cross a `${...}` template literal. **A mutation that doesn't land is indistinguishable from a gate that works.** Every mutation now asserts it changed the file before the test runs. This is the second time this week the lesson has been "the green tick was about something else".
**The honest bit:** Earlier in the same session I ran `git checkout` on a test file to undo a mutation and deleted three tests I'd written minutes before and hadn't committed. The suite went green either way. I only caught it because I grepped for the test names instead of trusting the run.
**Hook material:** "Two sweeps were written to fix back buttons. Both missed the same one. Not because anyone was sloppy — because the check searched for `<IconButton` and the bug was a `<div>`." Also: 35 of 143 buttons in the app override the button component's own padding, radius, font size or background. 16 of them override `background` — the single property the component exists to decide.
**Postable?:** yes — "your linter's anchor is your blind spot" is a genuinely useful post, and the hollow-falsification story is the honest half.

## 2026-09-27 — LOG-OFFPLAN-01 · the runs nobody counted
**Shipped:** A run the plan did not prescribe now counts toward actual weekly load and shadow load, and still cannot trigger an automatic reshape.
**Dev learning:** "Sum actual load per plan week" was hand-written in FIVE routes. The Coaching Board's ruling wasn't really a feature — it was a reason to finally give that sum an owner. The thing I'd tell another builder: when you split one value into two that mean different things, **delete the old field name instead of redefining it.** I removed `actualKm` and added `linkedKm` + `offPlanKm`, and TypeScript walked me to all six call sites including two test files. If I'd kept `actualKm` and quietly changed what it meant, every call site would have compiled and one of them would have been wrong forever.
**Product/creator learning:** The measurement inverted the thing everyone assumed. We all expected off-plan runs to be secret hard sessions — the runner sneaking in a fast one. They're shorter and *more* zone-disciplined than the sessions we prescribe (68.8% vs 60.0% in Z2). The grey-zone drift is in *our* prescriptions. That killed one board member's hypothesis and softened another's objection, and neither would have happened from reasoning about it.
**AI-building learning:** I gave the board a headline number — "65% of runs are off-plan" — and it was wrong by 2.4×. 79% of those runs **predate the user's plan**: HealthKit history imported on connect. The tell was sitting in my own per-user table (7 of 9 accounts had never linked a single run, and their run windows ended before their plan began) and I read straight past it, because the number was dramatic and confirmed what I was arguing. The fix is boring and mechanical: I now filter `start_date >= plans.created_at` inside the owner, with the reason in a comment. **Confident synthesis over a real query is still confident synthesis.**
**The honest bit:** Two self-inflicted ones. I quoted that 65% to a board that then reasoned on it — the ruling's direction survived but its urgency didn't, and I had to correct it in front of the founder. Then during falsification I ran `git checkout` on a test file to undo a mutation, forgetting the composed arms I'd added weren't committed yet, and silently deleted three tests I'd just written. Caught it because I checked `grep -c COMPOSED` rather than trusting the green run — which is the only reason it isn't still missing.
**Hook material:** "65% of our users' runs were invisible to the training engine. Then I checked the dates: 79% of them happened before the user had a plan. The real number was 26.9%." Also: the board's second clause turned out to already exist in the codebase — `buildShadowLoadAdjustment` copies the week unchanged and says *"Flagged — no auto-change applied."* We ruled on something we'd already built and forgotten.
**Postable?:** yes — the "my dramatic number was 2.4× wrong and the tell was in my own output" angle is the strongest thing here.

The 44px floor caught a real 29px button. `stickyScroller` flagged `inset: '162px 0 0'` as an unconstrained scrollport — it isn't, `inset` pins top and bottom, and the gate I wrote this morning didn't know. "Make it the width of the pill" turns the horizontal scale into exactly 1, so the squashing I was about to counter-scale away simply stops existing. "Make it part of the pill" turns a gap I'd tuned to 10px into an overlap of −26. Both times the simplification came from him.

That is my environment — but `Sheet.tsx` releases its enter animation on a bare rAF too, so a sheet mounting while the app backgrounds leaves the scrim up, the body scroll-locked, and no panel. The one he was looking at was my own regression: the conversion dropped `display: grid` as "owned by `.btn`", and `.btn` sets `inline-flex`, so the grid columns were inert. Same root as the "sign out is misaligned" report two rounds earlier — and **the gate I wrote for that class couldn't see this one**, because it checked `textAlign` plus `justifyContent` and this row *had* a `justifyContent`. What it had lost was `display`. A check aimed at one symptom of a cause misses the others.

**The honest bit:** my first attempt at that fix ran a `flexDirection` regex across the whole file and mangled 32 unrelated elements — the file didn't parse. Reverted in one command and redone by exact anchor, but it's a reminder that a regex edits by pattern, not by position, and will find things you didn't mean. Two existing tests also failed, correctly: they asserted ModifyPlanSheet renders its own cross, which is documented behaviour. The rule hasn't changed and now holds for every sheet, so both tests follow it to its new home.

**Hook material:** Our sheet component drew a drag-to-dismiss pill and listened for no touch events. Six screens inherited a gesture that didn't exist. Nobody noticed because the pill *looks* right — and the only way to find it is to try to swipe, which no test does and which nothing in this codebase has ever run on a device.

**Postable?:** yes

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — GHOST-AFFORDANCE-01 · 56% of the buttons had no surface

I counted: **74 of 131 controls — 56% — had no surface at all.** `ghost` had become the default variant not because anyone chose it but because it was the safest thing to convert a bare-looking button into. Collins' phrase for it is the one I'll keep: *absence dressed as restraint*. The rule that came out is positional — a primary action on its screen gets a surface, a control inside a sentence doesn't — because position is inspectable and importance isn't.

**Product/creator learning:** He reported "sign out button is misaligned". It was **eleven** controls. My conversion dropped each call site's `justifyContent` as "owned by `.btn`" — but `.btn` sets `justify-content: center` and these are row-shaped, so their labels silently centred. "Sign out" ended up centred directly above a left-aligned "Delete account" in the same card, which is how he spotted it. The class was right and my sweep was wrong: the rule is that a control declaring its own alignment keeps it.

**AI-building learning:** The board gave me a success condition — surfaceless below 50% — and I hit 51%. Reaching it would have meant sweeping ghosts the same ruling told me not to sweep. The two halves conflict, and the honest output is the number plus the conflict, not a sweep that technically satisfies a threshold. Same shape as the one-label-one-treatment rule, which is unmeetable alongside the positional rule as literally phrased, so the gate compares within a context and says so in its own comment.

**The honest bit:** The zones on Me were "all over the place" and the cause was three characters: `auto` in `gridTemplateColumns: '32px 1fr auto'`. Each row is its own grid, so every row sized its HR column to its own content and the numbers started at a different x on every line. I'd assumed `tabular-nums` was doing the aligning — it aligns digits *within* a cell and can do nothing across independent grids.

**Hook material:** More than half the buttons in my app had no surface at all. Not a design decision — the accumulated residue of always picking the safest conversion. The founder needed one sentence to spot what a variant census took to quantify: "Log manually does not look like a button."

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — BUTTON-GEOMETRY-01 · the founder looked at the app and found what four gates missed

**Shipped:** A size class is now a floor rather than a box, the controls I resized are back, and a geometry harness gates every future conversion.

**Dev learning:** `min-height: 48px` alone is a floor. `min-height: 48px` with `padding: 15px 20px` and `font-size: 14px` is a **box**, because padding and line-height set the height and the minimum never binds. I wrote a floor and shipped a box, and the syntax hid it from me. 20 of 32 converted controls changed height, −19px to +4px. The three that *shrank* were the only three whose code had reasoned about its own size — one carried the comment *"bigger than the 44pt min — primary ceremony CTA"* — so I overrode exactly the call sites that had made a decision and left alone the ones that hadn't.

**Product/creator learning:** The founder found this by opening the app. `tsc`, the ownership gate, the render tests and 3,527 suite tests were green throughout, and correctly so: every one of them asks *"does this use the right owner?"* and none asks *"does it still render the same box?"* That's a new failure class — **a refactor that normalises a distribution** — and the tell is a commit that deletes many differing literals and adds one shared class.

**AI-building learning:** I proposed converting one file and asking him to eyeball the screen. He asked why, and he was right: that's asking a human to do QA a check should do. The reason I reached for it is that I half-knew the harness had a hole and hadn't looked. I looked — **it never measured width**, which is what actually made the button huge. Worse, I'd "falsified" that arm by reinstating `fullWidth`, watching a test go red, and recording it as caught. It went red because the same edit removed two other classes. **A mutation that changes two things proves nothing about either.**

**The honest bit:** Five modelling bugs in that harness before I trusted it — blind to component usages, content-box in a border-box app, summing inline padding with class padding (reporting a 50px control as 80px), a regex that broke when I put a comment above a declaration, and no width at all. I also abandoned a 49-file restoration mid-build when I realised my verification was pairing the wrong elements, and reverted it rather than ship something unverifiable to live users. And I renamed a class within an hour of shipping it, because I'd named it after its first use again — third time in one day.

**Hook material:** My design system's button class said `min-height: 48px`. That reads like a minimum. It was a fixed size, because the padding underneath it set the height and the minimum could never bind. Twenty buttons changed size, four automated gates stayed green, and the founder found it by opening the app.

**Postable?:** yes

"Decrease whole distance" tells you what the button *does*; nothing told you what the number *became*. `role="spinbutton"` belongs on the readout, not the buttons, and that distinction is the whole fix. A VoiceOver user could press `+` and have no way to confirm the number they'd just set. Sierra's ranking was the right one: the tap count makes the app annoying, the silence makes it unusable.

**AI-building learning:** The most useful output of the sitting was a refusal. I'd have built the `Stepper` — it's a clean, obvious component, it would have passed every check, and it would have been a fifth numeric control on a product that already has four and a documented rule for choosing between them. The board also refused the *other* obvious move: swapping the stepper for a number input. Not because it's wrong, but because a `type="number"` brings the iOS focus-zoom trap that this very file carries a comment about four lines below the stepper, and nothing here has ever run on a device. Twenty-two taps to log a half-marathon is a real cost, and it's now accepted on the record rather than quietly fixed into a worse problem.

I'd been in that file four times today and hadn't noticed until I counted. Collins' line is the one I'd keep: *the pattern file is good and it is not being read.* So the fix wasn't another component, it was a routing table — one table saying which numeric control for which job, because the routing already existed in prose and nobody was finding it.

**Hook material:** I asked a design board to approve a component. They told me not to build it, pointed at a sentence already in our own pattern file, and then refused to let me build the obvious alternative either — because it would have traded 22 taps for an iOS keyboard bug we've hit before and can't test for. The best thing I shipped that hour was a table.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — ICON-BUTTON-01 · the component we needed was already there, wearing the wrong name

**Shipped:** `IconButton`, extracted as the generalisation of `BackButton`, with a required accessible name — plus names for the five controls that had none.

**Dev learning:** I went looking for a missing primitive and found a misnamed one. `BackButton` was already a 44px circle on `--bg-soft` with a mandatory label and its own contract — it *was* the general icon button. But it carried the name of one of its uses, so nothing else could reuse it without calling a close button a back button. Thirteen controls got hand-rolled instead, and `ModifyPlanSheet`'s close turned out to be byte-for-byte the documented spec, typed out a second time. That's the third instance today of the same shape: the right thing existed and was scoped wrong. `.cta-pill` was the same story this morning.

**Product/creator learning:** Five controls had no accessible name, and four of them are the distance stepper. A VoiceOver user on that screen hears "minus, plus, minus, plus" and has no way to know which number each one moves. That was the only part of the whole sitting that changes what a person can actually *do* — everything else was for us. Sierra's line in the room was the right one: don't let the tidy half carry the urgent half over the line. The names shipped independently of the component.

**AI-building learning:** The brief I took to the board was wrong, twice, in the flattering direction. I said 14 icon controls with 7 unnamed. My classifier stripped `{...}` expressions out of each button's body and then called anything textless an icon control — so a full-width zone row and a disclosure header, both carrying plenty of text, came back as "silent icon controls". The truth was 12 and 5. Third measurement I've had to correct today, and the fix wasn't to make the classifier cleverer: the gate now treats any `{expression}` body as possibly-labelled and skips it. It's biased toward passing and it says so in the comment, which is better than being confidently wrong about a count I'm briefing a decision on.

**The honest bit:** The refactor broke `backArrowOwner.test.ts`, which reads the 44px-circle spec out of `BackButton.tsx` — and my first instinct was to relax the assertion, because "the spec is still honoured, just elsewhere". That would have been the wrong move on a rule the register already records as *standing and ignored by half its instances*. I followed the values to the class that now owns them instead, kept every substitution, and added an assertion that `BackButton` still asks for the circle. The test failing was the system working.

**Hook material:** We had 13 hand-rolled icon buttons because the component that did exactly what they needed was called `BackButton`. Nobody wants to render a back button as a close icon. A naming decision made once, quietly, cost thirteen reimplementations — and one of them was byte-for-byte identical to the documented spec.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — BUTTON-MIGRATION-02 · the next batch found the hole in this morning's gate

**Shipped:** 90 of 217 controls now come from the shared button system, up from 41 — `secondary` ×14, `ghost` ×31, and two primary CTAs the gate had been completely blind to.

**Dev learning:** `--accent: var(--moss)`. It's a System B legacy alias that `globals.css` keeps on purpose, and two live primary CTAs used it with white text — the exact 3.68:1 contrast failure my gate was written to catch, and it matched neither arm. The check compared the token *name*; the producer used a different name for the same colour. The tempting fix is to add `--accent` to the pattern. The right fix is to stop maintaining a list at all: the gate now reads the `--x: var(--y)` alias graph out of the stylesheet and walks it transitively, so a legacy alias added next year is covered without anyone remembering. This repo has already written down that a checker sharing the producer's hand-written list is blind to that list in exactly the same way the producer is — I'd read that note and still shipped the list version.

**Product/creator learning:** I nearly turned 44 grey buttons green. The obvious move was to convert every text button to the `quiet` variant, which is moss. But `design-rulings.md:456` says *dismiss is never `--moss`* — moss is the CTA colour, and spending the strongest colour in the system on *dismiss* teaches the opposite of what it means. So the de-emphasised buttons needed their own variant. The thing that saved it was the settled-ground scan, not my judgement: I'd have called it a tidy-up and reversed a ruling **while the diff looked like a migration**.

**AI-building learning:** The warning I wrote to myself two hours earlier is what caught the real defect. When I filed the batch I wrote: *"those text buttons are not moss, so the gate says nothing about them — measure their contrast before converting, or the batch will look like a migration and quietly be an audit."* Measured: **4 of 51 were failing AA** — three `--warn` labels at 2.69:1 and a `--danger` at 4.36:1. Writing down the assumption is what made it get checked; without that line I'd have converted all 51 and moved on, and the contrast failures would have survived the migration that was supposedly cleaning them up.

**The honest bit:** I've now found a hole in this gate twice in one day — wrong line numbers this morning (because `^\s*//` matches `
` in JS and ate the blank lines above every comment), and the alias blindness this afternoon. Both were in a check I'd already falsified and called done. Falsifying against the defect you know about doesn't tell you about the one you don't. I also hit the `[...Map]` tsconfig trap that's documented in CLAUDE.md — second time this week.

**Hook material:** My contrast test was green over two buttons that were failing contrast. Not because the test was wrong — because the CSS said `--accent` and the test said `--moss`, and `--accent: var(--moss)` was one line away in the same stylesheet. The fix was to stop hardcoding the list and read the alias graph instead.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — WEBSITE-BUTTON-UNIFY-01 · the board threw out my framing and was right

**Shipped:** The marketing site's 3 CTAs now use the same `.btn` classes as the app, `.cta-pill` is deleted, and `Button.tsx` lost its `'use client'`.

**Dev learning:** I took the question to the Design Board as *"should the site import `Button`, with an `as` prop or a `ButtonLink` for the anchor case?"* Not one seat argued for it. The shared unit is the **class layer**, not the component — `Button.tsx` is thirty lines of prop-spreading, and every pixel of the design is in `globals.css`. One place to change how a button looks was already `globals.css`; I'd been about to build a React abstraction to prove a point that CSS had already made. And the framing turned out to matter technically as well as tidily: two of the three site CTAs live in **server** components, so importing a `'use client'` component into them would have pushed a client boundary onto a static page. That's `BUNDLE-BOUNDARY-01` — the class that took this homepage 110 kB → 249 kB and 114 kB → 251 kB, both times with nothing visibly wrong.

**Product/creator learning:** The measurement inverted the brief again. I'd told the founder the website was "the biggest visible gap" with ~14 controls. It's **3**, and two of the others were preview harnesses rendering app UI. But the smaller number made the finding *worse*, not better: `.cta-pill` only ever supplied hover/focus/press, so each of the 3 sites hand-typed its own font-size, padding, radius and label colour — and all three differed, one with a hardcoded `'white'`. Three buttons, three geometries, one shared hover. The site didn't have a button; it had three.

**AI-building learning:** The value of a board sitting isn't the verdict, it's that it forces the question to be stated precisely enough to be wrong. I wrote the brief as an options list — (a) unify onto Button, (b) keep two places, (c) something else — and the answer was in (c), which I'd included as a formality. If I'd just implemented (a), which was the obvious one and the one I'd have picked, it would have typechecked, passed every test, and shipped a client boundary onto a static marketing page.

**The honest bit:** The conversion introduced a defect that didn't exist before and I nearly didn't catch it: `btn--regular` is 48px tall with an 18px radius, and the waitlist input sitting beside it computes to 46px with a 14px corner. Two pixels and four pixels, in a side-by-side flex row. I only found it because I stopped to compute the input's box rather than assume the button slotted in. I also quoted a success condition ("distinct geometries 3 → 1") that I did not literally meet — there are still three declared variants, they just derive from one definition now. Reported it as measured rather than as promised.

**Hook material:** I asked five designers whether our website should import our button component. None of them said yes. The shared thing was never the component — it was the 40 lines of CSS the component points at. Building the "obvious" abstraction would have tripled the JavaScript on a static marketing page, silently, and every test would have stayed green.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — BUTTON-COMPONENT-01 · the buttons looked flat, and they also failed contrast

**Shipped:** One `Button` component, 41 controls converted across 17 files plus the email CTA, and every moss control that carries text now clears WCAG AA.

**Dev learning:** The founder said "the CTAs look very flat". The cause wasn't a missing shadow, it was that there was no Button component at all: 212 `<button>` elements, 66 carrying `--moss`, 27 of them the same nine-line inline style object written out again from whatever was nearby. `--shadow-lifted` had been sitting in `globals.css` with ZERO consumers while `--shadow-card` had 19 — the product elevated its cards and gave its buttons nothing, so the moss button sat visually *behind* the card it was on. Nobody ever made a button decision; they made it 27 times.

**Product/creator learning:** The real finding was underneath the one I was asked about. White on `--moss` is 3.68:1 and AA wants 4.5:1, so every primary CTA in the product failed contrast — and `A11Y-CONTRAST-01` had measured that exact failure months ago, shipped `--moss-strong` and `--moss-deep` to fix it, and then applied them to the **marketing** button only. 28 uses on the website. Zero in `app/dashboard`. Zero in `lib/email`. That reclassified the whole item from "polish when we get to it" to "has to ship", and it changed the staging argument: "convert nothing, let files be touched over time" is defensible when the cost is flatness and not when the cost is an accessibility failure.

**AI-building learning:** Three of my own decisions were wrong and only measuring caught them. (1) The board's ruling quoted one button as its reference — uppercase, 13px — so I made `.btn` force uppercase. Then I counted: **33 of the 40 controls being converted were NOT uppercase.** The cited example was the minority, and I'd have restyled 33 buttons nobody asked me to touch, inside a build whose whole job was to change one thing. A single quoted example is not a population. (2) I gave the `soft` variant `--moss-strong` because that's the AA token — it's 4.36:1 on a moss-tinted ground, still failing. The gentlest-looking variant needs the strongest ink. (3) My own gate reported real offenders at wrong line numbers twice, because `^\s*//` matches `
` in JS and swallowed the blank lines above every comment.

**The honest bit:** I shipped a check yesterday for hollow test shapes and it caught a hollow assertion in *this* check — `toContain('mossStrong')` passes against `mossStrongX`. The email theme's mirror map also rejected two colours I'd added before they were real tokens. Both of those are guards written earlier in the week catching me this week, which is the argument for writing them, but it is not a comfortable way to find out. I also read a suite result as green because the exit code said 0 while the summary said `1 failed` — the same "read the line, not the exit code" mistake in reverse.

**Hook material:** 3.68:1. That's the contrast of white text on our primary button, against WCAG's 4.5:1 minimum. The fix had been in the codebase for months — applied to the marketing site and never to the app. A test called `a11yContrast.test.ts` was green the entire time, and it wasn't wrong: it asserts the *token* is fine, which it is, and nothing had ever checked whether anything used it.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — TIME-INPUT-SECONDS-01 · asked to build a component that already existed

**Shipped:** every time field in the app collects seconds, and the decision left the call site.

Truncating always rounds a runner *faster* — 11.8 sec/km at 5K — and every prescribed pace is derived from that benchmark, in a product whose entire argument is that people run too hard. Defaulting would have left three call sites still passing an explicit value and three inheriting a new one, with nobody visiting either. The evidence that would settle it cannot exist until this ships, which is a good reason to write that down rather than pretend consensus.
**Hook material:** I was asked to build one component for consistency. It already existed, was already used everywhere, and already did the thing — behind a flag that half the screens forgot to set.
**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-25 — RECALIBRATE-ZONES-COOKIE-CLIENT-01 · we fixed the half of the sentence that had been reported

**Shipped:** a runner who has a plan can recalibrate again.
**Dev learning:** a real user entered a half-marathon time, tapped the button, and was told *"No plan found."* His plan is sitting in the `plans` table. The route authenticates off the Bearer token and then read the plan with the cookie client — on native there is no cookie session server-side, so the read hits RLS, comes back empty, and the 404 fires.
**Product/creator learning:** the part I keep thinking about is that we had already found this, on this route, eight days ago. `AUTH-BEARER-MISSING-01` fixed the client half — attach the Bearer, because *"cookie sync is unreliable on native"* — and that sentence has two halves. The client sends a token; the server then has to stop relying on a cookie. **We fixed the half that was producing a 401 because a 401 was what someone had reported, and left the half that produces a 404 because nobody had hit it yet.** The comment explaining the whole mechanism was sitting four lines above the call.
**AI-building learning:** the remedy existed in three sibling routes, one of which carries the explanation verbatim. So the useful check was not "what is wrong here" but "who else does this, and what do they do differently" — a four-route sweep that took a minute and made the fix obvious. That is the fourth time today the answer was a remedy that existed and had not been carried across.
**The honest bit:** the guard I shipped is a source check, not a behavioural one, and I want that on the record rather than implied. The failure needs a live RLS-enforcing database and a native client; no unit test can stand that up. What is mechanically checkable is that no plan-fetching route reaches for the cookie client, and that would have caught this one. Calling that "a regression test" without the caveat would be overclaiming.
**Also:** verified on the runner's actual stored plan rather than a fixture — 12 weeks fetched, 12 updated, paces moving 5:33–6:38 to 6:12–7:24. A fixture would have proved the code path; his plan proved the bug.
**Hook material:** the comment explaining exactly why this breaks was four lines above the line that broke, in a fix we shipped eight days earlier for the other half of the same sentence.
**Postable?:** yes

The charity migration five days earlier names `v_trial_conversion` **by name** in its own comment, explains that it would miscount comped runners, and then fixes a different view. The half that was written down got fixed; the half nobody had thought of — that the bias could run the *other* way, flattering us — was never looked for. **A defect you have described in prose is not a defect you have fixed, and describing it makes it feel handled.**
**AI-building learning:** I kept the raw `converted` column rather than correcting it in place. A view that silently changes what an existing column means is worse than one that is visibly wrong, because anything already reading it gets a new answer to an old question without being told. The new column is the one the gate reads; the old one stays, and a gap of more than one between them now means something real has changed.

**Hook material:** the trial conversion rate was 3.2% against a 5% target, and 100% of it was my own founder's comp account.
**Postable?:** yes

**Product/creator learning:** that last one is the one worth keeping. `foundation_week_violations` is computed as `errors.filter(v => (v.week ?? 1) <= 0)`. Foundation weeks carry *negative* week numbers. But `week: 0` is this codebase's convention for "plan-level, no specific week" — 60 emit sites, documented in a comment on the first one. So the field counts plan-level violations and calls them foundation weeks. Across the live fleet it reports 50; one is a foundation week and 49 are not. **A field whose name states a cohort and whose arithmetic counts a different one will mislead every single reader, and it had already misled the digest, the board item and me for the first twenty minutes.**

Achilles, Back, Hip, Shin splints and Plantar fasciitis fall between them. Same input, injury value varied: the healthy runner gets four delivered-volume warnings at +23%; the Back and Plantar-fasciitis versions reach **+36% in silence**. §94 exists *because* healthy runners had no delivered check — and its gate created the mirror hole for the cohort with more reason to be guarded. **Declaring an injury currently removes a check that declaring nothing would have given you.**

The engine's matcher was fixed for exactly this on 2026-09-16; the invariant's was not, and the invariant's comment still says *"Predicate matches the engine's injury-cap gate exactly."* It has been false for nine days. `invariant:liveness` cannot see it, because both invariants are **proven wakeable** — via `knee`. **Liveness proves a rule can fire. It cannot prove it fires for the cohort it names, and we have no harness for that.**

GTM-CHARITY-05's migration comment *named this exact failure* five days ago and then fixed only `admin_user_tiers`. At 30 users, one admin row is 3.2 points of a 5-point threshold.
**Hook material:** I was asked to cap a 41% jump that turned out to be correct, and found instead that five of the six injuries our own wizard offers get no volume check at all. The one that does is the one the digest did not mention.

## 2026-09-24 — GATE-FALSIFY-01 shape 3 · the lint missed a hollow test on the day it shipped

**Shipped:** the hollow-test lint now catches an assertion that has no input and therefore cannot fail.
**Dev learning:** the shape was `expect(() => guideArticles()).not.toThrow()` under a title about comparisons and principle references. The naive rule — flag any test whose only assertion is `not.toThrow()` — finds 18 of these in the repo and about 17 are perfectly good tests, because in this codebase throwing IS the domain signal: the generator throws on a designed refusal, the input validator throws on a rejected input. "Accepts a plausible runner" is *exactly* `not.toThrow()`. What separates them is the argument. `f(x)` asserts something about x. `f()` asserts nothing, because nothing varies.

Shape 1 started at 50 hits with 27 wrong. Shape 3 started at 18 with 17 wrong. Both times the first heuristic would have shipped a gate that cried wolf, and a gate that cries wolf gets switched off, which this repo has already recorded as identical to having no gate.
**AI-building learning:** the best falsification I have run. Rather than construct a synthetic case, I put the actual hollow test back into the actual file and watched the lint name it by file, line, title and expression, then restored it. No argument about whether the fixture was representative: it was the incident.
**The honest bit:** I wrote the detector with `matchAll`, which fails typecheck in this repo — and the function immediately above mine carries a comment explaining that exact error and why it uses an exec loop instead. I read that comment earlier in the session. Also: adding one test file tipped two unrelated borderline tests over the duration gate, which is a real finding rather than noise. They measure 1.6 seconds standalone and were sitting just under the line.
**Hook material:** the obvious version of this rule flags 18 tests and 17 of them are correct. The whole fix is one word: arguments.

## 2026-09-24 — BINGE-BUCKET-CROSS-01 · the build was red because a plan got better

**Shipped:** the plan-quality gate no longer reports an improvement as a regression.
**Dev learning:** `auditPlanQuality` emits `BINGE-SEVERE-75` at >=75% and `BINGE-WEEK` below — two buckets, one predicate. The baseline comparator scored every code independently with `n > b`. So when my own long-run cap earlier in the day moved one beginner marathoner from 75% to 74%, the severe bucket went 20 -> 19, the mild one went 281 -> 282, and the build failed on the `+1`. The fix is to compare declared families by cumulative sum from the most severe down: every prefix must hold, so `severe -1, mild +1` passes and `severe -1, mild +2` still fails. Membership is declared, never inferred from a shared prefix — `DAYS-SHORT` and `DAYS-SHORT-SILENCED` share one and are not severities.
**Product/creator learning:** the register is the point, not the green tick. I did not re-baseline. The debt is still 301 plans with a session over §52's share cap; what changed is that the gate can now read which direction it moved.
**AI-building learning:** I nearly re-baselined it. That is the reflex — the number moved, declare a reason, write the new number. Doctrine in this repo says exactly that, and it would have been wrong here: re-baselining would have recorded "the deload cap made BINGE-WEEK worse" when it made a runner's plan better. **Before you declare a move, find the one case that moved and look at it.** Diffing the case list took ten minutes and turned "declare and re-baseline" into "the comparator is broken".
**The honest bit:** it was red on main all day and I had run `npm run verify` more than once, reading the test line and not the exit code. That is the exact thing my own notes say to stop doing. It only surfaced because I piped to a file and echoed `$?` this time.
**Hook material:** `npm run verify` exited 1 for eleven hours because a training plan improved by one percentage point and crossed a bucket boundary.
**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-24 — PLAN-ZONE-VS-HRTARGET-01 · the bug was caused by the thing that fixes it

**Shipped:** correcting your heart rate now updates your sessions, not just your profile — and the three-copies-of-one-truth problem underneath it has a single owner.

**Dev learning:** The root cause and the fix were the same fact. `computeZones` lived **private** inside `ruleEngine.ts`, a server module. The dashboard needed the same arithmetic when a runner corrects their HR, couldn't reach it, and hand-rolled `Math.round(rhr + 0.70 * (mhr - rhr))` inline. Once a boundary formula exists in two places, one of them stops being updated — and that is exactly what happened: `meta` moved, the sessions didn't, and a card ended up showing 161–175 bpm above 158–171. The fix wasn't "also update the sessions", it was "make the arithmetic reachable so there's only one of it."

**Product/creator learning:** My analysis said two write paths. Reading them properly, there are **three**, and two of them deliberately never touch the plan — with comments saying why. I'd have quietly wired all three and reversed a documented decision while pushing an `observed` max (which §50 treats as a *floor*) into live plans. **I stopped mid-build and asked instead**, which is the difference between following the procedure and performing it.

And the backfill's refuse-on-new-violation guard **caught my own fix making a plan worse** — three plans carry `resting_hr: 0`, where Karvonen's reserve becomes the entire max; one went 2 → 6 violations and the script refused to write it. I would have shipped that.

**The honest bit:** `0` is a number. `computeZones(mhr, rhr?)` branches on `rhr === undefined` to pick §14's %MaxHR fallback, so a stored `0` takes the **Karvonen** branch with a zero baseline — the worst of both. I only found it because the dry run printed numbers that didn't improve, and I looked instead of shrugging at "7 → 7".

**Hook material:** A runner's card showed two different heart-rate ranges, six lines apart. The cause: one formula, written twice, because the original was in a file the screen couldn't import from.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-24 — GATE-FALSIFY-01 (a) · the rule that was written down three times and enforced zero

**Shipped:** a lint that fails the build on the two hollow test shapes this repo keeps writing, with all 19 existing instances fixed.

**Dev learning:** The most valuable part was not the detector, it was **measuring the false-positive rate before writing the rule**. The obvious heuristic — "this test file reads source, so `toContain` is substring-biased" — produced 50 hits of which **27 were wrong**, because `expect(fields).toContain('benchmark')` is array membership and the bias does not apply at all. Narrowing to *receiver assigned from `readFileSync`* took it to 23 with zero false; narrowing again to *positive assertions only* took it to 19. `.not.toContain` is the safe direction: substring bias makes a positive assertion too **weak** and a negative one too **strong**, and flagging the strong one would have added four false alarms. A gate that cries wolf gets deleted, which this repo already records as equivalent to having no gate.

**Product/creator learning:** I fixed all 19 rather than baselining them. The debt-register pattern is right when the backlog is 27 invariants or 20 contracts; at 19 one-line changes it is just deferral with paperwork. The gate ships green with nothing behind it to forget.

I only found it by running the lint across the whole repo before shipping, which is the thing I would have skipped if I had trusted the three unit cases I had just written. **A detector's unit tests tell you it works on the cases you thought of.**

**The honest bit:** this is the fourth hollow-check incident in one day and the first one where I built the gate instead of writing another note about it. The reason the class survived so long is visible in the file header: the rule existed in three documents, all of them true, none of them executable.

**Hook material:** "Falsify any new check before trusting it green." Written in the engineering doc. Written in the build procedure. Written in the debugging procedure. Enforced in zero places, while the build-log accumulated 15 hollow checks, 23 inert ones and 11 substring misses.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-24 — CHARITY-SEAT-MIGRATION-APPLY-01 · I handed over a verification query that could not fail

**Shipped:** the seat-stays-spent migration is live and verified; the migrations ledger records it.

**Dev learning:** I could not apply the migration myself (CLI unlinked, sandbox refuses production writes), so I gave the founder a query to prove it had landed: `pg_get_functiondef(...) like '%charity_codes%'`, `false` means applied. It came back `true` and I nearly concluded the migration had failed. It hadn't — **my replacement function names `charity_codes` three times in its own explanatory comments** (*"charity_codes.claimed_at IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLEARED HERE"*), so that query returns `true` in both states. The corrected probe matches the **statement**, `~* 'update\s+public\.charity_codes'`, which the new body genuinely never contains.

**Product/creator learning:** In the same exchange I misread *"no rows returned"* from the SQL editor as *"zero rows matched"*. It is what `UPDATE` without `RETURNING` always prints. So I told the founder a successful repair had failed, and then told them a successful migration might have failed, back to back — two wrong conclusions from two outputs I had not thought about carefully. **When you cannot run the command yourself, the quality of your verification instructions IS the quality of your work.**

**AI-building learning:** This is the third hollow check I caught today — after a falsification case with unreachable code after its assertion, and a contracts audit that could only validate contracts that already existed. The pattern is identical every time: *the check passes for a reason other than the one in its name.* The two I caught in my own code I caught by mutation-testing. **This one I could not mutation-test, because it ran on someone else's machine — which is exactly why it was the one that got through.** A query handed to a human is untested code.

**The honest bit:** the founder ran what I asked, reported accurately, and both of my readings of their results were wrong. They were right about the mechanism earlier too — the 2 → 1 count that I had waved off as a stale note turned out to be two shipped decisions cancelling each other out.

**Hook material:** I wrote a test to prove my own migration had applied. It returned "true" — failure — because my migration's comments mentioned the table it had stopped touching. The check was reading my explanation of the fix and reporting it as the bug.

**Postable?:** yes

## 2026-09-24 — CHARITY-REDEEM-RATELIMIT-01 + the CLAUDE.md line that understated what is live
